concept: the na't copies its head noun's case, not the reverse
prompt: A learner writes رَأَيْتُ الرَّجُلَ الطَّوِيلُ ('I saw the tall man'), leaving the adjective الطَّوِيلُ nominative while its head الرَّجُلَ is accusative. Name the required agreement axis, the error, and the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: The adjective (na't) must copy the case of its head noun (mawsūf): الرَّجُلَ is accusative as the object of رأيت, so the adjective must also be accusative, not nominative. The corrected sentence is رَأَيْتُ الرَّجُلَ الطَّوِيلَ.
accepted_variants: the adjective copies the case its head noun already carries; the head is accusative here, so the adjective must be accusative too, not nominative
case agreement between an adjective and its head noun means the adjective takes on the head's case; the head is accusative as the object, so the adjective must be accusative, not nominative
forbidden_answers: the adjective's case decides the head noun's case
the nominative adjective is correct regardless of the head's case
required_reasoning: the head noun identified as accusative (the object of the verb)
the adjective required to copy that case rather than assign its own
the corrected accusative adjective form given

concept: definiteness parity separates an attributive phrase from a complete predication
prompt: A learner reads الطَّالِبُ مُجِدٌّ ('the student is diligent') as the noun phrase 'the diligent student,' treating مُجِدٌّ as a na't of الطَّالِبُ. Explain why مُجِدٌّ cannot be a na't here and what the sentence actually says.
expected_answer: A na't must match its head noun's definiteness as well as its case, gender and number. الطَّالِبُ is definite (it carries the article) while مُجِدٌّ is indefinite, so the two cannot pair as head and attributive adjective. With no definiteness match, مُجِدٌّ is instead the khabar of a nominal sentence: الطَّالِبُ مُجِدٌّ is the complete sentence 'the student is diligent,' not the phrase 'the diligent student.'
accepted_variants: mujiddun here is the khabar of a complete nominal sentence, not a na't of al-talib, because the definite head and the indefinite mujiddun cannot pair as head and attributive adjective
since al-talibu is definite and mujiddun is indefinite, the definiteness mismatch means this is a full predication, not the noun phrase 'the diligent student'
forbidden_answers: mujiddun here is a na't of al-talib forming the phrase 'the diligent student'
definiteness does not matter for na't agreement
required_reasoning: definiteness identified as a required agreement axis alongside case, gender and number
the mismatch between the definite head and the indefinite mujiddun noted
the correct reading given as a complete predicate sentence, not a noun phrase

concept: a non-human plural head is modified as feminine singular
prompt: A learner modifies the non-human plural الْكُتُبَ بَ ('the books') with the masculine sound-plural adjective الجَدِيدِينَ, writing رَأَيْتُ الْكُتُبَ الجَدِيدِينَ. Explain the agreement rule this violates and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: A non-human (ghayr ʿāqil) plural noun is modified as if it were feminine singular, regardless of the noun's own gender or the plural pattern it uses; a masculine sound-plural adjective is reserved for human referents. الْكُتُبَ is non-human, so its adjective must be feminine singular: الجَدِيدَةَ. The corrected sentence is رَأَيْتُ الْكُتُبَ الجَدِيدَةَ.
accepted_variants: a non-human plural noun takes a feminine-singular adjective regardless of its own gender or plural pattern; a masculine sound plural adjective belongs only to human referents
since al-kutuba is non-human, its adjective must be feminine singular (al-jadidata), not a masculine sound plural
forbidden_answers: a masculine sound plural adjective is correct for any plural noun regardless of referent animacy
al-kutuba al-jadidina is the correct agreement here
required_reasoning: the head noun classified as a non-human referent

the corrected feminine-singular adjective given

concept: genitive case alone cannot settle attachment inside an idāfa chain
prompt: A learner insists that the genitive case of الطَّوِيلِ by itself proves it modifies بَيْتِ (the house) and not الرَّجُلِ (the man) in the annexation chain مِفْتَاحُ بَيْتِ الرَّجُلِ الطَّوِيلِ. Explain why case alone cannot settle the attachment here, and state the correct discipline.
expected_answer: In a chain of muḍāf/muḍāf ilayh, every member after the first bears the genitive, so the genitive case of الطَّوِيلِ matches BOTH بَيْتِ and الرَّجُلِ, and both candidates are masculine singular, so gender and number do not break the tie either. With no further evidence, the attachment is genuinely undecidable from the sentence alone: it could describe the tall house or the tall man, and the case ending gives no way to choose one. Naming one attachment as certain from the case ending alone forces a choice the evidence cannot license; the honest answer is that both readings stay open pending context.
accepted_variants: every non-initial member of an idafa chain is genitive regardless of which one is modified, and here both candidate heads also match in gender and number, so the case ending alone cannot decide the attachment; both readings must be preserved rather than forced

forbidden_answers: the genitive case ending proves al-tawili modifies bayti and not al-rajuli

required_reasoning: every non-initial member of the chain recognized as genitive regardless of which one is modified

concept: an indefinite, non-annexed attributive elative stays in its invariable base shape
prompt: A learner modifies the indefinite feminine head طَالِبَةٌ with the feminine-inflected elative form فُضْلَى, writing طَالِبَةٌ فُضْلَى مِنْ زَمِيلَتِهَا intending 'a female student better than her classmate.' Explain why the elative must stay in its base masculine-singular shape here, and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: As an indefinite attributive follower with no article and no annexation, the elative (afʿal-pattern) stays in its invariable base shape, أَفْضَلُ, regardless of the head noun's gender or number — it still agrees with the head in case and definiteness, but it does not copy gender or number here. The feminine pattern فُضْلَى belongs to the definite or annexed uses, not to this indefinite comparative use. The corrected sentence is طَالِبَةٌ أَفْضَلُ مِنْ زَمِيلَتِهَا.

concept: an intended attributive phrase needs BOTH definiteness parity and case agreement
prompt: A learner wants to say 'I greeted the tall man' and writes حَيَّيْتُ الرَّجُلُ طَوِيلٌ, intending الرَّجُلُ طَوِيلٌ to read as the definite phrase 'the tall man' functioning as the object. Explain what is missing and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: Definiteness parity is part of what licenses a na't reading, not just case: with الرَّجُلُ left nominative and طَوِيلٌ indefinite, the pair does not read as one definite accusative object phrase at all — it reads as a stranded predication, not the intended object. To get the phrase 'the tall man' as the object of حَيَّيْتُ, the adjective must match the head in BOTH definiteness and case: الرَّجُلَ الطَّوِيلَ (both definite, both accusative). The corrected sentence is حَيَّيْتُ الرَّجُلَ الطَّوِيلَ.

concept: plural agreement for a non-human referent is governed by animacy, not the singular's own gender
prompt: A learner modifies the non-human plural الْجِبَالَ ('the mountains') with the human masculine sound-plural الشَّاهِقِينَ, reasoning that جَبَل ('mountain') is a masculine noun in the singular. Explain why the singular's gender is irrelevant here and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: Plural agreement for a non-human referent is governed by ANIMACY, not by the grammatical gender of the singular form. جَبَل is masculine in the singular, but that does not carry over to plural agreement, because الْجِبَالَ denotes non-human things: a non-human plural is modified as feminine singular regardless of the singular noun's own gender. The corrected sentence is رَأَيْتُ الْجِبَالَ الشَّاهِقَةَ.

concept: the correction connector بَلْ after negation confirms the first negation and affirms the second term
prompt: A learner writes مَا كَتَبَ زَيْدٌ الدَّرْسَ بَلْ مَا قَرَأَهُ, adding a second مَا after بَلْ, intending 'Zayd didn't write the lesson; rather, he read it.' Explain why the second negation is redundant and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: بَلْ after a negated first clause CONFIRMS that first negation — it does not cancel or retract it — and affirms the second element positively instead. Adding a further مَا after بَلْ negates the very element بَلْ was meant to affirm, so the sentence ends up (wrongly) denying both writing AND reading instead of confirming the first negation while affirming the second. The corrected sentence keeps the first negation standing and states the second element positively: مَا كَتَبَ زَيْدٌ الدَّرْسَ بَلْ قَرَأَهُ.
accepted_variants: bal after a negated clause confirms and keeps that first negation standing while asserting the second element positively; re-negating the second element with another ma states the opposite of what bal was meant to do
bal does not cancel the first clause's negation after a negated clause, it confirms it, and affirms the second element instead; the corrected clause following bal must stay affirmative
forbidden_answers: the corrected clause after bal must also be negated to match the first clause

bal after a negated clause cancels or retracts the first negation entirely

concept: a coordinated conjunct copies the case of the element it is joined to
prompt: A learner writes نَجَحَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرًا, marking the conjunct عَمْرًا accusative even though زَيْدٌ is the nominative subject of نَجَحَ. Name the rule this violates and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: A coordinated conjunct copies the case of the element it is joined to (the maṭūf ʿalayh); it never carries a case of its own. زَيْدٌ is nominative here as the subject of نَجَحَ, so the conjunct عَمْرٌ must also be nominative, not accusative. Marking it accusative breaks the case-inheritance relation and leaves the two joined terms with mismatched exponents. The corrected sentence is نَجَحَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرٌو.
accepted_variants: the conjunct must copy the head's case rather than carry one of its own; zaydun is nominative, so the joined amrun must also be nominative, not accusative
case-following means the second coordinated term takes the same case as the first; since zaydun is nominative, amrun must be corrected from accusative to nominative
forbidden_answers: a coordinated conjunct may carry a case different from the element it joins
amran accusative is correct here regardless of zaydun's case
required_reasoning: the case-inheritance rule stated: the conjunct copies the head's case
zaydun identified as nominative

concept: light لكن only coordinates a single word after negation/prohibition; before an independent clause it is a non-governing adversative
prompt: A learner sees لكن in حَضَرَ زَيْدٌ لكن عَمْرٌو غَائِبٌ ('Zayd came, but ʿAmr is absent') written with no shadda on the nūn, and insists it must still be governing عَمْرو's case — either as the heavy abrogator's accusative ism, or as a light coordinator copying زَيْدٌ's nominative case onto عَمْرو. Explain why light لكن governs nothing here, and give the correct case and reason for عَمْرٌو.
expected_answer: Light لكن (no shadda) only COORDINATES a single following word, and only when it follows a negation or prohibition. Neither the heavy abrogator's accusative ism marking nor a light coordinator's case-copy can be right here: there is no negation before لكن, and لكن is followed by an entire independent clause (عَمْرٌو غَائِبٌ), not one word, so لكن cannot be functioning as a coordinator at all, light or heavy. Before an independent clause it is a non-governing adversative/ibtidāʾ particle. عَمْرٌو is nominative simply because it is the mubtadaʾ of its own following nominal sentence, never by any case inherited from لكن.
accepted_variants: neither the heavy abrogator's accusative ism marking nor a light coordinator's case-copy applies here, since there is no negation before lakin and a full independent clause follows it rather than one word; amrun is nominative as the mubtada of its own clause, not from lakin

an accusative ism marking would only fit the heavy abrogator, and a case-copy would only fit the light coordinator, but neither condition is met since lakin here precedes a whole clause with no prior negation; amrun's nominative case comes from its own role as mubtada, not from lakin
forbidden_answers: the un-geminated lakin still governs its ism into the accusative exactly like the heavy abrogator
the shape of the nun makes no difference to whether lakin coordinates or governs a case

required_reasoning: light lakin's licensing conditions (following a negation/prohibition, before a single word) checked and found absent here
lakin therefore identified as a non-governing adversative/ibtidaʾ particle before this independent clause, not a coordinator, light or heavy

concept: the plain additive وَ asserts no order; a sequencing connector is needed when order matters
prompt: A learner uses the plain additive وَ in دَخَلَ زَيْدٌ وَخَرَجَ عَمْرٌو intending that Zayd's entering happened BEFORE ʿAmr's leaving. Explain why the intended sequencing is unrecoverable here and name the correct connector.
expected_answer: وَ is a plain additive connector: it joins two events with no claim about their relative order, so a reader cannot recover which happened first from وَ alone. When the ordering itself is part of the intended message, a sequencing connector is required instead: ثُمَّ marks that the second event follows the first. The corrected sentence is دَخَلَ زَيْدٌ ثُمَّ خَرَجَ عَمْرٌو.
accepted_variants: wa asserts plain addition with no order between the two events, so when the order matters, thumma must replace wa to mark that the second event follows the first
since wa carries no ordering claim at all, the intended before/after sequence cannot be recovered from it; selecting thumma is required whenever order is part of the message
forbidden_answers: wa asserts that the first event happened before the second

required_reasoning: wa's lack of any ordering claim identified

a sequencing connector (thumma) selected because the order matters

concept: فَ asserts a tight, no-interval sequence and cannot host a stated gap
prompt: A learner writes تَزَوَّجَ زَيْدٌ فَوُلِدَ لَهُ وَلَدٌ بَعْدَ عَشْرِ سَنَوَاتٍ, using فَ even though the sentence itself states a ten-year gap between the two events. Explain the contradiction and give the corrected connector.

concept: position between two terms confirmed, then the conjunct still copies the head's case
prompt: A learner writes سَافَرَ الطَّالِبَانِ وَالْمُدَرِّسَيْنِ, leaving the dual conjunct الْمُدَرِّسَيْنِ accusative even though الطَّالِبَانِ is the nominative dual subject of سَافَرَ. Explain the discriminator test and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: Position between two terms is the first discriminator for a coordinator: once وَ is confirmed as joining two nominal terms rather than two clauses, the conjunct always copies the case of the term it is joined to. الطَّالِبَانِ is nominative (dual) as the subject of سَافَرَ, so the conjunct الْمُدَرِّسَانِ must also be nominative dual, not accusative dual. concept: a coordinating لا between two terms negates only the second term, not the clause
prompt: A learner reads the لا in زَيْدٌ حَاضِرٌ لا غَائِبٌ ('Zayd is present, not absent') as ordinary clause negation, as if it negated the whole predication from the front. Explain why its POSITION here marks it as a coordinator instead, and what it actually negates.

concept: after an affirmed clause, بَلْ signals idrab (redirection within one discourse thread), not a plain contrast between unrelated facts
prompt: A learner uses بَلْ in زَيْدٌ حَاضِرٌ بَلْ عَمْرٌو غَائِبٌ intending a plain contrast between two different people. Explain the mismatch with بَلْ's actual force after an affirmed clause and name the correct connector.
expected_answer: After an AFFIRMED first clause, بَلْ signals إِضْرَاب — the speaker turns away from the first statement to redirect focus onto the second, without cancelling the first — within a single connected discourse thread, never as a way to introduce an unrelated fact about a different subject. Here the two clauses are simply separate facts about two different people, with no such redirection relation between them, so بَلْ misrepresents the connection. The adversative لَٰكِنْ is the connector for a plain contrast between unrelated statements: زَيْدٌ حَاضِرٌ لَٰكِنْ عَمْرٌو غَائِبٌ.
accepted_variants: bal after an affirmed clause signals idrab, redirecting focus to the second statement within one discourse thread without cancelling the first; two unrelated facts about two different people call for the adversative lakin instead
since the two clauses share no redirection relation, only two unrelated facts about different people, bal's idrab force does not fit; lakin is the correct plain-contrast connector here
forbidden_answers: bal after an affirmed clause is a plain contrast connector with no idrab/redirection force
zaydun hadirun bal 'amrun gha'ibun correctly expresses a plain contrast between two people
bal after an affirmed clause always means 'not only x but even more so y' about the same claim
required_reasoning: bal's idrab/redirection force after an affirmed clause identified (turning focus to the second statement within one discourse thread, not cancelling the first)

concept: with no interrogative marker at all, the choice between أَمْ and أَوْ is attributed, not forced
prompt: A learner insists that زَيْدٌ مُسَافِرٌ أَمْ عَمْرٌو, written with no هَلْ or أَ interrogative marker at all, must be a question and that أَمْ is simply wrong without one, demanding it be replaced with أَوْ. Explain why the choice between the two particles cannot be forced here.
expected_answer: أَمْ is the classical particle for an alternative QUESTION and is normally licensed by a preceding interrogative (هَلْ or أَ); أَوْ is the ordinary declarative alternation particle. With no interrogative marker at all, the clause type itself is not settled by the sentence as given, and grammarians differ on how strict this requirement is in practice, so the choice between أَمْ and أَوْ here is a genuinely disputed case. Forcing either replacement claims a certainty the evidence does not support; the correct discipline is to record both the question and the declarative alternation as attributed, unresolved readings rather than picking one.
accepted_variants: am's normal licensing by an interrogative marker is missing here, but that alone does not settle the clause type; grammarians dispute this case, so both readings must be preserved as attributed and unresolved rather than forcing aw
since no interrogative marker settles whether this is a question or a declarative alternation, the choice between am and aw is a disputed case that should stay attributed and unresolved, not forced
forbidden_answers: am is always wrong without an overt interrogative marker and must be replaced by aw
the choice between am and aw here is settled and only one reading is grammatical
required_reasoning: am's normal licensing by an interrogative marker named
aw's role as the plain declarative alternation particle named
the absence of an interrogative marker here recognized as leaving the clause type unsettled
the dispute preserved as attributed/unresolved rather than forced to one side

concept: a part-apposition (badal baʿḍ min kull) is not a quality-describing na't
prompt: A learner treats نِصْفُهُ in اِحْتَرَقَ الْبَيْتُ نِصْفُهُ ('the house burned down — half of it') as a quality-describing modifier of الْبَيْتُ and marks it accusative, the way a describing word might be. Explain why this is a part-apposition, not a quality reading, and give the case it must actually carry.
expected_answer: نِصْفُهُ is not a describing adjective; it is a noun (with a resumptive clitic pointing back to الْبَيْتُ) standing as a badal baʿḍ min kull — نِصْف names a literal physical part/fraction of الْبَيْتُ, the whole. A quality-marking accusative would fit an adjective, not this badal, which instead copies the case of its antecedent. Since الْبَيْتُ is nominative here (fāʿil of اِحْتَرَقَ), نِصْفُهُ must be corrected to nominative as well.
accepted_variants: a quality-marking accusative would fit an ordinary adjective, not this badal; nisfuhu is a noun with a resumptive clitic naming a literal part of al-baytu, and it copies al-baytu's nominative case

marking nisfuhu accusative would treat it as a quality-describing adjective; the part-vs-quality test instead shows it names a literal fraction of the whole and copies the antecedent's nominative case
forbidden_answers: nisfuhu is an ordinary quality adjective of al-baytu and should be accusative
a badal ba'd min kull takes an accusative of its own instead of copying the antecedent's case
nisfuhu is a badal ishtimal naming an abstract attribute of al-baytu rather than a literal part
required_reasoning: nisfuhu identified as a noun with a resumptive clitic naming a literal part/fraction of the whole, not an adjective and not an abstract attribute
the part-vs-quality test applied (a literal physical fraction of the antecedent, not a contained quality)
the badal's case tied to copying the antecedent's case, here nominative, not accusative

concept: a total apposition needs no resumptive clitic
prompt: A learner attaches a resumptive clitic to a total apposition, writing هَذَا صَدِيقِي زَيْدُهُ instead of هَذَا صَدِيقِي زَيْدٌ ('this is my friend, Zayd'), reasoning that every appositive needs a linking clitic. Explain why a total apposition needs no clitic here and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: صَدِيقِي and زَيْدٌ already denote the SAME entity in a total apposition (badal muṭābiq): the second noun simply restates the first with no part-whole or containment relation to link back to, so no resumptive clitic is needed. Attaching one anyway creates a spurious possession reading that does not belong to a total apposition at all. The corrected sentence is هَذَا صَدِيقِي زَيْدٌ, with زَيْدٌ unattached.
accepted_variants: a total apposition names the same entity as its antecedent, so no resumptive clitic is needed; attaching one to zaydun here produces a spurious possession reading
since sadiqi and zaydun denote the same entity, the clitic is reserved for the part and inclusion types, not this total apposition, so the corrected form drops the clitic
forbidden_answers: every appositive requires a resumptive clitic linking it back to the first noun
zayduhu is the correct form of a total apposition
required_reasoning: the total apposition identified as denoting the same entity as its antecedent
the resumptive clitic rejected as needed only for the part/inclusion badal types
the corrected clitic-free total apposition given

concept: an appositive must carry the same case as its antecedent
prompt: A learner marks the appositive pair accusative in نَجَحَ الطَّالِبَانِ خَالِدًا وَسَعِيدًا, reasoning it names a specific object. Name the rule this breaks and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: Marking خَالِدٌ وَسَعِيدٌ accusative would treat the apposition as an independent object, but an appositive (badal) must instead copy its antecedent's case. الطَّالِبَانِ is nominative here as the subject of نَجَحَ, so the appositives must be corrected to nominative as well.
accepted_variants: marking khalidun wa-sa'idun accusative would treat the apposition as an independent object; an appositive copies the antecedent's case instead, and al-talibani is nominative
an accusative marking on khalidun wa-sa'idun breaks case identity with the antecedent; since al-talibani is nominative, the appositives must stay nominative too
forbidden_answers: the appositive khalidun wa-sa'idun should be accusative because it names a specific object
an appositive may carry any case independent of its antecedent
required_reasoning: case identity between antecedent and appositive named as the required rule
the antecedent identified as nominative here
the accusative marking rejected as breaking the identity relation

concept: an apposition specifies identity; a na't predicates a quality
prompt: A learner labels خَالِدًا in قَابَلْتُ صَدِيقِي خَالِدًا ('I met my friend, Khalid') as a na't (descriptive follower) of صَدِيقِي. Explain why this is an apposition, not a description, and what test tells the two apart.
expected_answer: A na't predicates a QUALITY of its head (a property the head has); an apposition (badal) instead specifies IDENTITY or delimits reference — it names WHO or WHAT the first noun actually is. خَالِدًا does not describe a property of صَدِيقِي; it names the specific individual صَدِيقِي refers to, so the relation is identity, not description. The test is to ask whether the second word names a property of the first (na't) or names the referent itself (badal); here it names the referent, so خَالِدًا is a badal, not a na't.
accepted_variants: khalidan names who sadiqi actually is, an identity relation, not a property of sadiqi, so it is a badal rather than a na't
the identity-vs-quality test shows khalidan specifies the referent's identity rather than predicating a property, which makes it a badal, not a na't
forbidden_answers: khalidan describes a quality of sadiqi and is therefore a na't
there is no test that distinguishes an apposition from a descriptive follower
required_reasoning: the quality-vs-identity distinction between na't and badal stated
khalidan recognized as naming the referent's identity, not a property
the correct classification (badal, not na't) given with its test

concept: a partitive apposition needs a resumptive clitic linking back to the whole
prompt: A learner omits the resumptive clitic in the partitive apposition, writing أَعْجَبَنِي الْكِتَابُ نِصْفٌ instead of أَعْجَبَنِي الْكِتَابُ نِصْفُهُ ('the book amazed me -- half of it'). Explain why the clitic is required here and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: In a partitive or inclusion apposition, the second noun names only a PART or an included aspect of the first, so without a formal link back to the antecedent, the pair reads as a different construction entirely. A resumptive clitic that resolves back to the substituted-for noun is required: نِصْفُهُ ('half of it'). The corrected sentence is أَعْجَبَنِي الْكِتَابُ نِصْفُهُ.
accepted_variants: nisf names only a part of al-kitab, so the partitive apposition needs a resumptive clitic resolving back to it; the corrected form is nisfuhu, not bare nisfun
without a clitic linking back to al-kitab, the partitive reading is lost; the required correction attaches the clitic as nisfuhu
forbidden_answers: the partitive apposition needs no resumptive clitic linking it back to the antecedent
nisfun bare, with no clitic, correctly expresses 'half of the book' here
required_reasoning: nisf recognized as naming only a part of al-kitab, not the whole
the resumptive-clitic requirement for the partitive type stated
the corrected clitic-bearing form given

concept: animacy is a strong cue toward coordination, not an absolute gate against accompaniment
prompt: A learner insists that الْحَرَسَ (an animate noun) can never be a wāw al-maʿiyya accompaniment object, forcing خَرَجَ الْأَمِيرُ وَالْحَرَسَ into a coordination reading even though the intended sense foregrounds the prince as the one who went out, with the guard merely accompanying. Explain why animacy alone cannot force the coordination reading.
expected_answer: Animacy is a strong CUE toward coordination (two agents jointly performing an action), not an absolute GATE that rules out accompaniment: an animate noun can still be construed as accompanying rather than co-acting when the speaker foregrounds one actor as the one who acts and treats the other as merely present alongside. Here the intended sense foregrounds الْأَمِيرُ as the actor with الْحَرَسَ merely accompanying, so the accompaniment reading is licensed and الْحَرَسَ takes the accusative: خَرَجَ الْأَمِيرُ وَالْحَرَسَ, with الْحَرَسَ accusative.
accepted_variants: animacy is only a strong cue toward coordination, not an absolute gate, so an animate noun can still be an accompaniment object when one actor is foregrounded
since al-amiru is foregrounded as the actor here, al-harasa can still be construed as accompanying rather than co-acting, licensing the accusative accompaniment reading despite being animate
forbidden_answers: an animate noun can never be an accompaniment object under wa al-ma'iyya
animacy alone always forces the coordination reading regardless of which actor is foregrounded
required_reasoning: animacy identified as a strong cue rather than an absolute gate
the foregrounded-actor test applied to license accompaniment despite animacy
al-harasa correctly assigned the accusative accompaniment case

concept: the wāw al-maʿiyya accompaniment object is accusative, never a second nominative subject
prompt: A learner writes جَلَسَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرٌو intending 'Zayd sat together with ʿAmr' (an accompaniment reading), but leaves وَعَمْرٌو nominative. Explain the case this role requires and give the corrected sentence.
expected_answer: زَيْدٌ stays nominative as the subject of جَلَسَ, while the wāw al-maʿiyya requires its accompaniment object عَمْرًا to be accusative.
accepted_variants: zaydun is nominative as the subject, and the accompaniment object after wa al-ma'iyya must be accusative; leaving amran nominative instead reads as plain coordination, not accompaniment
zaydun stays nominative as the subject, but the accompaniment object amran must be accusative, not a second nominative like a coordinated subject
forbidden_answers: the accompaniment object after wa al-ma'iyya stays nominative like a second subject
jalasa zaydun wa-'amrun already expresses accompaniment
required_reasoning: the accompaniment reading distinguished from plain coordination
zaydun confirmed nominative
the accompaniment object correctly assigned accusative, not nominative

concept: when both nominals can jointly perform the verb, coordination is the default reading
prompt: A learner marks عَمْرًا accusative in خَرَجَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرٌو, reading it as accompaniment, even though both زَيْدٌ and عَمْرٌو can equally well be described as jointly performing خرج with nothing foregrounding one over the other. Explain which reading is the default here and give the decisive test.
expected_answer: Where joint performance of the verb is available to both nominals and nothing foregrounds one actor over the other, the default reading is plain coordination, not accompaniment: apply the participation test first (can both nominals equally perform the action together?) before committing to accompaniment, and let the CASE marking itself be the decisive evidence, not an assumed accompaniment sense. With no foregrounding, عَمْرٌو stays nominative, agreeing with زَيْدٌ as a second joint subject: خَرَجَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرٌو.
accepted_variants: with no foregrounded actor, joint participation makes coordination the default; case marking decides, and amrun stays nominative rather than being marked accusative for accompaniment
the participation test is applied before assuming accompaniment; since both can jointly perform the action with nothing foregrounded, amrun is corrected back to nominative
forbidden_answers: accompaniment is the default reading whenever two nominals could jointly perform the verb
amran accusative is correct here even with no foregrounded actor and no accompaniment sense signaled
required_reasoning: the participation test (can both nominals jointly perform the action) applied
coordination named as the default when nothing foregrounds one actor
case marking treated as the decisive evidence, amrun kept nominative

concept: a maʿiyya accompaniment object needs a verbal governor to its left
prompt: A learner marks الْكِتَابَ accusative in the bare nominal string الطَّالِبُ وَالْكِتَابَ (no verb anywhere), claiming an accompaniment reading 'the student with the book.' Explain why maʿiyya cannot be read here and give the correct case.
expected_answer: Wāw al-maʿiyya would need a verbal governor to license the accusative accompaniment reading, but الطَّالِبُ وَالْكِتَابَ has no verb anywhere. With no governor, the wāw defaults to plain coordination, and الْكِتَابُ must be corrected to nominative, copying الطَّالِبُ's own case.
accepted_variants: an accusative accompaniment reading needs a verbal governor that is missing here, so the wa defaults to coordination and al-kitabu copies al-talibu's nominative case
the absence of any verbal governor rules out the accusative accompaniment reading; the corrected reading is plain coordination with al-kitabu nominative
forbidden_answers: wa al-ma'iyya can govern an accusative accompaniment object with no verb anywhere in the sentence
al-kitaba accusative is correct here even though there is no verbal governor
required_reasoning: the absence of any verbal governor identified
the accompaniment (ma'iyya) reading rejected for lack of a governor
the bare nominal sequence resolved as plain coordination with the second noun copying the first noun's nominative case
